title: Beliefs and Boredom
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that student boredom is best remedied by the simplest effective solution rather than by gamifying or individualizing an entire curriculum. His claim is that boredom is highly individual and flows from a student's beliefs about a task, specifically the Belonging/Identity and Effort/Value beliefs, among the five he treats as the roots of motivation. He illustrates with himself: anime bores him and teaching blogs do not, though neither is inherently boring, because his identity and valuing differ for each. The piece concludes that studying the five beliefs and their research-backed interventions is more efficient than revamping a whole school.
points: Boredom produces disengagement, either not doing the work or doing it with little attention and care, so it is worth treating at the level of cause.
Gamifying all of education is a far more complicated undertaking than applying research on the five key beliefs beneath student motivation.
Nothing is inherently boring: Stuart finds anime dull and teaching blogs fascinating purely because of different beliefs about each.
Belonging/Identity and Effort/Value are the two beliefs he uses to explain why the same activity bores one person and absorbs another.
Loving something is a high form of the value belief, which explains why years of effort toward teaching never felt like a burden to him.
quotes: When students get bored, they disengage from the task at hand. They either don't do the work — of listening, of learning, of reading, of writing — or they do it with a very low level of attention and care.

To remedy student boredom, I argue that the simplest solutions are the best ones. It's certainly possible that gamifying all of education is a way to remedy student boredom — but I think this is a much more complicated undertaking than, say, studying the five key beliefs beneath student motivation
After all, boredom is highly individualized. While you may find it interesting to read blogs about teaching, most people in the world would find that tediously boring.
I would argue that anime is no more inherently boring than teaching blogs are. It's just that I have one set of beliefs about anime and another about teaching.
(Loving something is a high form of the value belief.) Teaching also feeds my family — so I value getting better at teaching from a utilitarian perspective, too.

So what I would say to someone who is seeking to combat student boredom by revamping their whole curriculum or school into something gamified or intensely individualized is that it might be more efficient to bone up on the five key beliefs first. The research is rich, and many of the interventions are simple.
